# The Leftover Screws

## I. The Body in the Key

Before the body, the gymnasium.

It was a sound first—always a sound first in a room built to magnify them—the particular drone of fluorescent tubes that had been burning all night, a sixty-hertz hymn that the first player to push through the double doors at 5:47 a.m. registered in her sternum before her eyes adjusted. Then the smell, which was not death but its opposite: floor polish, rubber dust, the ghost-sweat of ten thousand possessions and fast breaks baked into the hardwood's grain over a decade, a smell so specific to this one building, this one court in the Garland Heights Athletic Complex, that any of the eight women on the Garland Wheels roster could have been blindfolded, wheeled into the room, and named it before their tires crossed the threshold. The echo architecture was cathedral-strange. A shout from the baseline took 1.3 seconds to return from the steel rafters, distorted, hollowed, as if the building were answering in a voice it had taught itself. A basketball's bounce, that metronomic knock of rubber on polyurethane, traveled the room's geometry in overlapping waves that the players had learned to read with the unconscious fluency of bats navigating a cave. This was a space designed for motion—for the squeal of quick-release axles in tight pivots, for the particular thunder of a fast break executed in sport wheelchairs whose cambered wheels turned the athletes into something between cyclist and centaur, for the grunting collisions under the basket where position was fought for with shoulders and trunk strength and the shameless leveraging of momentum. Every surface existed to amplify the body in motion.

Which is what made the still body so wrong.

Marcus Aimes lay on his back inside the painted key, that trapezoidal territory under the home basket where the lane lines converged in faded blue. His arms were at his sides. His legs—which had not moved voluntarily since a spinal infection seventeen years ago took the signals away somewhere between his T-4 and T-5 vertebrae—were straight, his feet in their perpetual slight outward rotation, his sneakers (he wore sneakers always, out of what he called professional solidarity) clean and double-knotted. His eyes were closed. A dark contusion wrapped the left side of his skull above the ear like a hand that had tried to hold his head together and failed. There was blood, but not the volume the movies promise; it had pooled and stopped, a lake the size of a salad plate on the hardwood, already browning at its edges with the patience of an old stain.

His wheelchair—not his everyday chair with the scratched armrests and the Garland Wheels bumper sticker, but the spare, the meticulously maintained backup that he kept tuned to tournament specifications so that any player whose chair broke mid-game could transfer into it and keep playing—was folded neatly against the first row of bleachers, thirty feet away. Its wheels were aligned. Its anti-tip casters pointed forward. It leaned against the blue plastic seat at the precise angle that Marcus himself preferred for storage, the angle he'd demonstrated to a hundred people over a hundred setups and teardowns, the angle that protected the axle plate. Someone had folded it with care. Someone who had either watched Marcus fold chairs many times or who had, after killing him, taken the time to do it properly, which was either the same thing or something worse.

Raya Chowdhury was the one who found him. She had come early, as she did every Tuesday and Thursday, to run passing drills against the wall—a solitary exercise she told no one about, because the team's point guard admitting she needed to work on her outlet passes was a vulnerability she could not afford, not this close to the district championship. She had wheeled through the double doors, felt the hum, smelled the polish, and then seen the shape on the floor that was not a shape that floors are supposed to contain, and her first conscious thought—the one she would never tell anyone, the one that arrived before grief or shock or even recognition—was: *If practice is cancelled, I lose the wall time.*

She screamed. She called 911. She called Coach Davenport. She called Delivia, because Delivia was the team's center and emotional anchor and the person you called, and within twenty minutes the team had gathered in the doorway of the gymnasium in a ragged semicircle of wheelchairs and morning coats and undone hair, and every one of them wore the same expression—the slackened jaw, the wet unfocused eyes, the pulled-back posture of a body that wants to retreat from what the brain has processed—and beneath each identical mask, a private machine was running:

Raya, in her black track jacket with the reflective piping, was already calculating—the distance from the bleachers to the body, the effort required to fold a sports wheelchair, the logistics of entry after the building's 10 p.m. lockdown, the fact that the fluorescent lights were on, which meant either someone had a key or someone had never left. Delivia Robinson, the center, six-foot-one even seated, her broad hands gripping her push rims so hard the tendons in her wrists stood out like bridge cables, was remembering something she had seen—Marcus in the lobby two days ago, his phone to his ear, his lips shaping words she had read because she always read lips, had read them since she was nine years old and the hearing in her left ear departed without explanation and the hearing in her right ear became a negotiation rather than a guarantee, and what his lips had shaped was a sentence she had not yet told anyone. Anh Nguyen, the shooting guard, the quietest player on the roster, the one who bit the skin around her thumbnails during timeouts and never spoke in team huddles unless spoken to, had already retreated one wheel-length from the group and was texting her mother at Saint Clare's, not about the murder but about a shift swap, or so the text's first line claimed, though the second line asked a question about emergency room records that had nothing to do with scheduling. And Tomás Verdejo, the bench player, the twelfth and final name on a twelve-person roster—Tomás, whose game minutes this season totaled forty-one across seventeen contests, who sometimes appeared in the background of the team's promotional photos and sometimes did not, whose jersey number the PA announcer had called wrong as recently as last Saturday—was not looking at the body. He was looking at the doors. The main double doors, propped open with a rubber wedge that was not school-issued. The fire exit at the southeast corner, closed but—he could see from here—not fully latched. The equipment room door, shut, its key-card reader blinking green, which meant it was unlocked, which meant either the last person to use it had failed to lock it or someone had used a card after hours and the system hadn't reset.

Tomás catalogued these details and told no one, because no one asked, because no one ever thought to ask Tomás what he'd noticed.

The police arrived. The gymnasium was sealed. The team was moved to the hallway, where the echo was different—shorter, deader, the sound of a space that didn't know what it was for—and a detective with a shaving cut on his chin took statements while behind the yellow tape two technicians knelt beside Marcus Aimes and did their work with the impersonal kindness of people who encounter the dead more often than they would like.

Marcus's everyday wheelchair was not in the building. That detail did not make the first round of statements.

The folded spare leaned against the bleachers, precise as a thesis.

## II. The Arrest and the Point Guard's Itch

Terrence Volke was arrested at 11:20 a.m. in his apartment on Masselin Avenue, four miles from the Garland Heights Athletic Complex, wearing sweatpants and a T-shirt from a basketball camp he'd coached six years prior, and he confessed before the detective with the shaving cut had finished reading him his rights.

"I did it," he said, reportedly, according to the local affiliate's 6 p.m. broadcast, which displayed his mugshot—a gaunt face, hollowed by two years of unemployment and custody hearings, with eyes that looked less like a killer's than like a man who had been expecting a knock on his door for a long time and was grateful, in the ruined way that only the very tired can be grateful, that it had finally come. "I went there. I hit him. I killed him."

It went together like furniture from a box. Tabs into slots. Allen wrench, dowel, cam lock. No sawdust. No leftover screws.

The motive assembled itself with the same obliging neatness: Volke had been the head coach of the Eastbridge Bolts, Garland's crosstown rival, until a district game two years ago when he lost a controversial charging call in the final minute and erupted—not at the referee, which would have been ordinary, but at Marcus, who had been running the score table for the home team and who Volke accused, on the record, into a live microphone, of manipulating the game clock. The tirade included language that the league's incident report described as "profane, personal, and targeting the victim's disability," and Volke was fired the next week by a school board that had been looking for a reason and finally had one they could print. He'd been sending Marcus emails for months afterward—emails the police now had—that started as apologies and curdled, over time, into the vinegar of a man who had decided his ruin was someone else's fault.

By evening, the machinery of relief was running at full speed: the principal of Garland Heights, Linda Foss, who had spent the morning on the phone with the district's liability counsel, terrified that the murder would expose the gymnasium's outdated keycard system and the maintenance budget she'd redirected to SAT prep materials, released a statement expressing sorrow and confidence in the police. The parents of the Garland Wheels players received a form email from the school counselor offering sessions and assuring them that "the individual responsible has been apprehended and poses no further threat to the school community." The district league commissioner, who needed the championship game to proceed on Saturday because the venue contract was non-refundable and the local news had already sold ad time against the broadcast, called Coach Davenport personally to express condolences and, in the same breath, to confirm that the team intended to play. The team itself, in a group chat that moved too fast for anyone to type a complete sentence, expressed what looked like consensus: it was Volke, obviously it was Volke, they'd always known he was unhinged, and the best way to honor Marcus was to win the championship in his name. The chat was full of hearts and prayer-hand emojis and the particular italicized earnestness of people who have been given permission to stop thinking about something frightening and have accepted the permission with both hands.

Raya Chowdhury, in her bedroom on the second floor of her parents' apartment on Devereaux Street, watched the 6 p.m. broadcast on her laptop, the screen's blue light turning her face into a mask she would not have recognized. She pressed pause on the mugshot. She pressed play. She pressed pause again.

She said, aloud, to no one: "He drove there at night. In a rage. With no plan. Found the gym unlocked—or what, broke in? Hit Marcus with—what? The police didn't say what. Folded the wheelchair. Folded it *neatly*. Left the lights on. Drove home. Went to bed. And then confessed six hours later like he'd been waiting for it."

Tabs into slots. No leftover screws.

But there were screws. She could feel them in her pocket.

She opened a notebook—a green composition book, college-ruled, the same kind she used for game prep, where she diagrammed opponents' pick-and-roll tendencies and charted referees' foul-call patterns by quarter—and at the top of the first blank page she wrote a word she immediately scratched out, then wrote again, smaller, in the margin, where it could be missed: *TIMELINE*.

While she wrote—dates, times, the sequence of the evening as the news had reported it, the gaps, the questions—the omniscient record of Raya Chowdhury requires the inclusion of a fact she had shared with no one and intended to share with no one and which shaped, like a gravitational body too massive to see, the orbit of every thought she'd had since 5:47 that morning:

Two weeks ago, on a Thursday, after a practice in which she'd scored eighteen points in a controlled scrimmage and Coach Davenport had called her "the best pure passer in the district," Marcus Aimes had asked her to stay behind in the equipment room. He closed the door. He pulled from a manila folder a photocopy of her functional classification paperwork—the document that established, through a battery of physical assessments, that her spinal cord injury limited her trunk function to a degree that placed her in the 1.0 player class, the most restricted, the class given to athletes with the least physical function, whose presence on the court was regulated by a point system designed to ensure competitive balance. Every team fielded five players whose combined classification points could not exceed a certain total. A 1.0 player was the most "valuable" in roster construction—she took up the fewest points, leaving room for more physically able teammates, and any team that had a genuine 1.0 who could also play like a 3.0 had an almost unfair advantage.

Raya was that advantage. Raya was the reason the Garland Wheels were in the championship. And Marcus, holding the paperwork under the equipment room's single buzzing bulb, had shown her, with the quiet, almost apologetic precision of a man who maintained machines for a living and could not tolerate a misaligned part, that her classification was wrong. Not ambiguously wrong, not wrong in the way that disability classification is always somewhat subjective—wrong in the way that required someone to have lied. Her trunk function assessment had been conducted by a physical therapist selected and paid by Coach Davenport. The scores on the assessment did not match the scores from her own medical records at the rehabilitation center where she'd been a patient since she was eleven. The discrepancy was not subtle. Someone had upgraded her disability on paper—made her appear more limited than she was—so that she would be classified lower, so that the team's point total would stay under the cap, so that Garland could field the lineup that was now, two weeks before the championship, the most dominant in the district.

"I'm giving you until after the championship," Marcus had said. "Then I go to the league. You can come with me or not, but I'm going."

She'd asked him why he was waiting at all, and he'd looked at her with an expression she wanted to call merciful but which she suspected was something colder and more strategic—the expression of a man who also loved the team and wanted the championship and was fighting himself—and he said, "Because Delivia deserves to play that game. The rest of you can sort yourselves out after."

Now Marcus was dead, and the deadline was meaningless, unless the paperwork still existed, unless someone else knew, unless the investigation—the real investigation, not the one the police had already closed by lunchtime—uncovered the classification fraud on its way to uncovering the murderer, in which case the deadline was not meaningless but detonated, a bomb with its timer removed, capable of going off at any moment or never.

Raya wrote in her notebook. She circled the word *FOLDED*. She underlined it. She circled it again.

The killer had folded the wheelchair. Had folded it the way Marcus folded wheelchairs. Which meant the killer knew Marcus, had watched Marcus, had spent enough time in the gymnasium to internalize a habit so specific that it functioned as a signature.
